planting.note: Anchor unweighted cuttings loosely in pea gravel or plant in submerged pots of heavy garden soil capped with sand, then lower into 1-3 ft of water once temperatures warm.

directions: Plant bunched, weighted stem cuttings directly into submerged containers of heavy loam topped with pea gravel to keep them anchored; new roots form quickly from the stem nodes. This fast-growing submerged oxygenator competes with algae for nutrients and shelters fish fry, but it spreads aggressively and is regulated or banned as invasive in some states, so confine it to contained water features and never release it into natural waterways. Thin regularly by pulling out handfuls of stems, and overwinter tender specimens indoors in cold climates since hard freezes kill top growth to the crown.

planting.note: Divide rooted crowns and plant in a submerged aquatic pot of heavy garden loam, then set the pot 6-18 inches below the water surface so the small heart-shaped leaves can float and spread.

directions: Pot divisions in loam-filled aquatic containers topped with gravel and submerge them so the mottled, lily-pad-like leaves reach the surface and produce clusters of small fringed yellow flowers through summer. It spreads by both rhizomes and floating stem fragments, so keep it confined to a container in ponds and remove excess growth each season to prevent it from choking open water; it is listed as invasive in parts of North America outside its native Eurasian range. Overwinter the rootstock below the ice line in the pond, since dormant crowns tolerate hard freezes as long as they do not dry out.

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in spring and plant 2-4 inches deep in a submerged pot of heavy loam set at the pond margin in up to 6 inches of standing water.

directions: Set rhizome divisions into containers of heavy garden soil and place them at the pond edge in shallow water, where the rush-like foliage sends up tall stalks topped with umbels of pink, three-petaled flowers in mid to late summer. It thrives in the same shallow marginal zone as pickerelweed and sagittaria and tolerates both standing water and periodic drying. Because it spreads by rhizome fragments and bulblets and is classified as a noxious aquatic weed in several US states and Canadian provinces, confine plantings to pots and check local regulations before adding it to a pond.

planting.note: Plant rooted runners in shallow aquatic pots of loam so the clover-like leaflets can either float on the surface or stand just above shallow water.

directions: This low-growing aquatic fern produces distinctive four-leaflet fronds resembling a four-leaf clover and spreads by creeping rhizomes across mud or shallow water at the pond margin. Plant divisions in submerged or bog-margin containers of heavy soil, and trim back runners regularly since it forms a dense mat that can overtake open water in mild climates. It is a useful low, textural contrast plant next to taller marginals like pickerelweed or Louisiana iris, and dies back to a hardy rhizome that survives freezing in the pond mud.

planting.note: Scatter a handful of the tiny floating fern directly onto the pond surface after the water has warmed; no planting medium is needed since it floats freely and multiplies on its own.

directions: This tiny free-floating fern forms a dense carpet of overlapping scale-like fronds that shade out algae and turn reddish in strong sun or cool weather. Simply toss a starter mat onto the water; it doubles rapidly through vegetative fragmentation and needs no rooting medium. Skim off excess growth regularly to prevent it from completely covering the surface and cutting off oxygen exchange, and treat it as an annual in cold climates since it is killed by hard freezes, though warm-region growers should check local rules as it can be weedy in mild-winter ponds and waterways.

planting.note: Float a small starter clump on the pond surface once nights stay reliably above 50°F; it needs no soil or anchoring and will multiply on its own in warm water.

directions: Water spangles is a free-floating fern with paired oval fronds covered in water-repellent hairs that trap air and keep the plant buoyant, plus a submerged root-like frond that absorbs nutrients. It provides quick surface shade for fish ponds and helps suppress algae, but reproduces so quickly by fragmentation that it is best grown in a contained water feature and skimmed out regularly rather than an open pond. It is frost-tender and collapses at the first hard freeze, so treat it as a seasonal annual outside USDA zone 9 and dispose of excess plants in the trash rather than a waterway, since it is a regulated invasive species in parts of the southern US.

planting.note: Scatter a small starter colony of fronds directly onto still pond water; it requires no soil and establishes itself within days in nutrient-rich water.

directions: Each duckweed plant is a tiny single leaf-like frond with a fine hanging root, and colonies double in population every few days under warm, nutrient-rich conditions, making it one of the fastest-multiplying pond plants available. It is prized in water gardens for outcompeting algae for excess nutrients and for providing forage and cover for fish and waterfowl, but a full pond surface should be avoided since a complete duckweed cover blocks light and oxygen exchange for submerged life. Skim off surplus fronds with a net every week or two during the growing season, and expect it to die back in winter in cold climates while overwintering as dormant turions in pond sediment in USDA zone 3 and warmer.

planting.note: Plant divisions in a submerged aquatic pot of heavy loam set 2-8 inches below the water surface once water temperatures are consistently warm.

directions: Water poppy produces glossy, rounded floating leaves and cheerful three-petaled yellow flowers that open in succession just above the water through summer, giving a long season of bloom in a small water-lily-like package. Grow it in a submerged pot of heavy garden soil topped with gravel, positioned in full sun in shallow to moderately deep water, and divide the spreading rhizome every year or two to keep it in bounds. It is frost-tender and will not survive a freeze, so gardeners north of USDA zone 9 should overwinter a potted division indoors in a bright spot or heated greenhouse and treat it as a seasonal pond annual otherwise.
